Determining a parabolic-elliptic-elliptic system by boundary observation of its non-negative solutions under chemotaxis background

Yuhan Li Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, P.R. China Affiliation: yuhli2-c@my.cityu.edu.hk    Hongyu Liu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, P.R. China    Catharine W. K. Lo Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, 518061, P.R. China Affiliation: hongyu.liuip@gmail.com, hongyliu@cityu.edu.hk Affiliation: catharinelowk@gmail.com, cwklo@szu.edu.cn
Abstract

This paper addresses a profoundly challenging inverse problem that has remained largely unexplored due to its mathematical complexity: the unique identification of all unknown coefficients in a coupled nonlinear system of mixed parabolic-elliptic-elliptic type using only boundary measurements. The system models attraction-repulsion chemotaxis—an advanced mathematical biology framework for studying sophisticated cellular processes—yet despite its significant practical importance, the corresponding inverse problem has never been investigated, representing a true frontier in the field. The mixed-type nature of this system introduces significant theoretical difficulties that render conventional methodologies inadequate, demanding fundamental extensions beyond existing techniques developed for simpler, purely parabolic models. Technically, the problem presents formidable obstacles: the coupling between parabolic and elliptic components creates inherent analytical complications, while the nonlinear structure resists standard approaches. From an applied perspective, the biological relevance adds another layer of complexity, as solutions must maintain physical interpretability through non-negativity constraints. Our work provides a complete theoretical framework for this challenging problem, establishing rigorous unique identifiability results that create a one-to-one correspondence between boundary data and the model’s parameters. We demonstrate the power of our general theory through a central biological application: the full parameter recovery for an attraction-repulsion chemotaxis model with logistic growth, thus opening new avenues for quantitative analysis in mathematical biology.  

Keywords: Nonlinear parabolic-elliptic-elliptic system; chemotaxis; mixed-type equations; unique identifiability; simultaneous recovery; multiplicative separable form. 
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 35R30, 92-10, 35Q92, 35B09, 35K99, 35J99

1 INTRODUCTION

1.1 Biology background and motivation of our study

Nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) systems play a central role in the mathematical modeling of biological processes involving spatial organization and collective behavior. A particularly influential example arises in the study of chemotaxis—the directed movement of cells or organisms in response to chemical gradients. Such systems are fundamental for understanding a wide range of biological phenomena, including bacterial aggregation, immune response, embryonic development, and tumor growth. This section introduces a class of chemotaxis models that form the basis of our study, beginning with classical formulations and progressively extending to more complex frameworks that incorporate multiple chemical signals and growth dynamics.

The mathematical foundation of chemotaxis modeling was established in the 1970s through the pioneering work of Keller and Segel [13, 14, 15]. Their models were derived from empirical observations of bacterial movement in response to chemical attractants, capturing the tendency of cells to aggregate and form spatial patterns. The classical Keller-Segel model consists of a pair of reaction-diffusion equations that describe the interaction between cell density and chemoattractant concentration. It incorporates both random diffusion and advective transport due to chemotactic drift:

{∂tu=duΔu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+f(u),∂tv=dv​Δ​v+α​u−β​v,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=d_{u}\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+f(u),\\ \partial_{t}v=d_{v}\Delta v+\alpha u-\beta v,\end{cases} (1.1)

where u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) denotes the cell density and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) denotes the concentration of the chemoattractant. The positive parameters dud_{u} and dvd_{v} represent diffusion rates, χ\chi is the chemotactic sensitivity, and f⁡(u):[0,∞)→ℝf(u):[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} is a smooth function satisfying f⁡(0)≥0f(0)\geq 0, often accounting for intrinsic growth or decay.

In many biological scenarios, the timescales of cellular motion and chemical diffusion can be significantly different. Chemoattractants such as nutrients or signaling molecules often diffuse much faster than cells can migrate, reaching a quasi-steady state almost instantaneously compared to the relatively slow redistribution of the population. This scale separation motivates a reduced yet biophysically relevant formulation.

A common simplification under the assumption of fast chemical diffusion leads to the parabolic-elliptic Keller-Segel system:

{∂tu=duΔu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+f(u),0=dv​Δ​v+α​u−β​v.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=d_{u}\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+f(u),\\ 0=d_{v}\Delta v+\alpha u-\beta v.\end{cases} (1.2)

This version is mathematically more tractable and effectively describes long-term behavior in situations where the chemoattractant reaches equilibrium much faster than the cell population. It has been widely analyzed [2, 31, 7, 1, 6] and applied to model biological phenomena such as nutrient-guided migration and stable pattern formation [13, 14, 8].

In many biological contexts, the relative timescales of cellular response and chemical diffusion are not fixed but may vary depending on environmental conditions or specific biological mechanisms. For instance, in certain developmental processes or under pathological conditions, the diffusion properties of signaling molecules may change, altering the dynamic coupling between cells and their chemical environment. This variability necessitates a modeling framework that can seamlessly transition between different dynamical regimes, thereby providing a more flexible tool for theoretical investigation and numerical simulation.

To bridge these diverse dynamical scenarios and incorporate variable timescale separations into a single analytical framework, one may introduce a switching parameter τ\tau that unifies the fully parabolic and parabolic-elliptic formulations:

{∂tu=duΔu−χ∇⋅(u∇v)+f(u),τ​∂tv=dv​Δ​v+α​u−β​v,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=d_{u}\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+f(u),\\ \tau\partial_{t}v=d_{v}\Delta v+\alpha u-\beta v,\end{cases} (1.3)

where τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}. Setting τ=1\tau=1 recovers the fully time-dependent system (1.1), while τ=0\tau=0 yields the parabolic-elliptic system (1.2). This integrated framework facilitates the study of systems across different time-scale separations.

In many biological contexts, however, cells respond to more than one chemical signal—often integrating both attractants and repellents to navigate complex environments. This dual response mechanism is crucial for numerous physiological and ecological processes, such as immune cells coordinating movement toward inflammatory signals while avoiding inhibitory factors, or microbial populations exploring resource gradients while evading toxic regions. The ability to process competing cues enables finer spatial organization and more adaptive collective behavior than single-signal systems can capture. To model this richer, more biologically realistic behavior, the attraction-repulsion chemotaxis framework has been developed:

{∂tu=Δu−∇⋅(χu∇v)+∇⋅(ξu∇w),in ​Q,τ​∂tv=Δ​v+α​u−β​v,in ​Q,τ​∂tw=Δ​w+γ​u−δ​w,in ​Q.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(\chi u\nabla v)+\nabla\cdot(\xi u\nabla w),&\text{in }Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}v=\Delta v+\alpha u-\beta v,&\text{in }Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}w=\Delta w+\gamma u-\delta w,&\text{in }Q.\end{cases} (1.4)

Here, vv represents an attractive signal (e.g., nutrients or chemoattractants) while ww corresponds to a repulsive one (e.g., toxins or repellents). The parameters χ\chi and ξ\xi quantify the strengths of chemotactic attraction and repulsion, respectively, allowing the model to represent a wide spectrum of biological phenomena. Such models have been used, for instance, to describe quorum sensing in bacterial colonies, where populations modulate movement in response to self-secreted attractants and waste byproducts [32], as well as microglial cell behavior in Alzheimer’s disease, involving response to both amyloid-beta attractants and repulsive signals in neural tissue [30]. From a mathematical perspective, these systems exhibit rich dynamics including pattern formation, phase separation, and critical transitions. Analytical results concerning global existence, boundedness, and blow-up of solutions can be found in [25, 29, 34, 26, 12].

While the attraction-repulsion framework captures essential aspects of bidirectional chemical response, real biological populations are further regulated by intrinsic growth constraints and resource limitations. In vivo and in vitro experiments frequently observe that cell proliferation is self-regulated through density-dependent mechanisms, such as contact inhibition or nutrient depletion, which prevent unlimited growth and ensure population sustainability. To incorporate these critical ecological features and better align the model with experimentally observed behaviors, we extend the system by including logistic-type growth terms. This extension not only enhances the biological fidelity of the model but also introduces important mathematical structure that can suppress blow-up phenomena and promote global existence of solutions.

In this paper, we focus on an extended version of the attraction-repulsion model that includes logistic growth terms:

{∂tu=Δu−∇⋅(χu∇v)+∇⋅(ξu∇w)+ru−μu2,in ​Q,τ​∂tv=Δ​v+α​u−β​v,in ​Q,τ​∂tw=Δ​w+γ​u−δ​w,in ​Q,∂νu=∂νv=∂νw=0,on ​Σ,u(x,0)=f(x),v(x,0)=g(x),w(x,0)=h(x),in ​Ω.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(\chi u\nabla v)+\nabla\cdot(\xi u\nabla w)+ru-\mu u^{2},&\text{in }Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}v=\Delta v+\alpha u-\beta v,&\text{in }Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}w=\Delta w+\gamma u-\delta w,&\text{in }Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}u=\partial_{\nu}v=\partial_{\nu}w=0,&\text{on }\Sigma,\\ u(x,0)=f(x),\quad v(x,0)=g(x),\quad w(x,0)=h(x),&\text{in }\Omega.\end{cases} (1.5)

Here, Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≥2n\geq 2) is a bounded Lipschitz domain, Q:=Ω×(0,∞)Q:=\Omega\times(0,\infty) is the space-time cylinder, and Σ:=∂Ω×(0,∞)\Sigma:=\partial\Omega\times(0,\infty) is its lateral boundary. These notations will be used consistently throughout the paper, including in the more general formulation (1.9) introduced below.

The logistic term r​u−μ​u2ru-\mu u^{2} in (1.5) introduces density-dependent proliferation and death, crucial for modeling population saturation and carrying capacity – features that are fundamental to ecological modeling and essential for realistic long-term behavior. The positive parameter rr represents the intrinsic growth rate, while μ\mu quantifies the strength of intra-specific competition. This extension not only enriches the biological relevance of the model but also significantly influences its analytical properties, often ensuring global existence of solutions and preventing uncontrolled growth. Well-posedness and qualitative properties of this and related systems have been studied in works such as [36].

Let B:={χ,ξ,r,μ,α,β,γ,δ}B:=\{\chi,\xi,r,\mu,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\} denote the set of biological parameters. We define the measurement operator:

ℳB+​(f,g,h)=((u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t),w⁡(x,t))|Σ,u⁡(⋅,T),v⁡(⋅,T),w⁡(⋅,T)),x∈Ω.\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B}(f,g,h)=\big((u(x,t),v(x,t),w(x,t))|_{\Sigma},\ u(\cdot,T),\ v(\cdot,T),\ w(\cdot,T)\big),\quad x\in\Omega. (1.6)

The associated inverse problem is then formulated as:

ℳB+→B,\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B}\to B, (1.7)

where the superscript ‘++’ emphasizes that we consider non-negative solutions biologically relevant for population densities. We are again concerned with the issue of unique identifiability: for two configurations B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}, does the following hold?

ℳB1+=ℳB2+if and only ifB1=B2.\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B_{1}}=\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B_{2}}\quad\text{if and only if}\quad B_{1}=B_{2}. (1.8)

A rigorous statement of this corollary is provided in Section 1.3.

1.2 Mathematical setup

Building upon the biological foundation established above, we now present the precise mathematical framework investigated in this work. We consider the following coupled nonlinear parabolic-elliptic-elliptic system:

{∂tu=Δu−∇⋅(χu∇v)+∇⋅(ξu∇w)+F(x,u),in ​Q,0=Δ​v+G⁡(x,u,v),in ​Q,0=Δ​w+H⁡(x,u,w),in ​Q,∂νu=∂νv=∂νw=0,on ​Σ,u(x,0)=f(x),v(x,0)=g(x),w(x,0)=h(x),in ​Ω,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(\chi u\nabla v)+\nabla\cdot(\xi u\nabla w)+F(x,u),&\text{in }Q,\\ 0=\Delta v+G(x,u,v),&\text{in }Q,\\ 0=\Delta w+H(x,u,w),&\text{in }Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}u=\partial_{\nu}v=\partial_{\nu}w=0,&\text{on }\Sigma,\\ u(x,0)=f(x),\quad v(x,0)=g(x),\quad w(x,0)=h(x),&\text{in }\Omega,\end{cases} (1.9)

where the domain Ω\Omega, the space-time cylinder QQ, and the lateral boundary Σ\Sigma are as defined below (1.5). The functions F⁡(x,m):Ω×ℝ→ℝF(x,m):\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} and G⁡(x,m,z),H⁡(x,m,z):Ω×ℝ×ℝ→ℝG(x,m,z),H(x,m,z):\Omega\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} are real-valued with respect to the variables mm and zz.

System (1.9) represents a generalized attraction-repulsion chemotaxis model where the chemical equations are assumed to reach equilibrium rapidly relative to cellular dynamics. Biologically, u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) denotes the population density of cells or microorganisms, while v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) and w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) represent the concentrations of a chemoattractant and chemorepellent, respectively. The parameters χ>0\chi>0 and ξ>0\xi>0 quantify the strengths of attraction toward vv and repulsion from ww, capturing the bidirectional chemical response mechanism discussed in Subsection 1.1.

More generally, the system can be formulated with variable time-scale separation through the introduction of parameters τ1,τ2∈{0,1}\tau_{1},\tau_{2}\in\{0,1\}:

{∂tu=Δu−∇⋅(χu∇v)+∇⋅(ξu∇w)+F(x,u),in ​Q,τ1​∂tv=Δ​v+G⁡(x,u,v),in ​Q,τ2​∂tw=Δ​w+H⁡(x,u,w),in ​Q,∂νu=∂νv=∂νw=0,on ​Σ,u(x,0)=f(x),v(x,0)=g(x),w(x,0)=h(x),in ​Ω.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(\chi u\nabla v)+\nabla\cdot(\xi u\nabla w)+F(x,u),&\text{in }Q,\\ \tau_{1}\partial_{t}v=\Delta v+G(x,u,v),&\text{in }Q,\\ \tau_{2}\partial_{t}w=\Delta w+H(x,u,w),&\text{in }Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}u=\partial_{\nu}v=\partial_{\nu}w=0,&\text{on }\Sigma,\\ u(x,0)=f(x),\quad v(x,0)=g(x),\quad w(x,0)=h(x),&\text{in }\Omega.\end{cases} (1.10)

Setting τ1=τ2=0\tau_{1}=\tau_{2}=0 yields the parabolic-elliptic-elliptic system (1.9), while τ1=τ2=1\tau_{1}=\tau_{2}=1 corresponds to a fully parabolic system. Our analysis encompasses both scenarios, with results applicable to this broader framework.

The central inverse problem addressed in this paper concerns the determination of unknown coefficients χ,ξ\chi,\xi and nonlinear functions FF, GG, and HH from boundary and final-time measurements. Formally, we define the measurement operator:

ℳχ,ξ,F,G,H+​(f,g,h)=(u⁡(x,t)|Σ,v⁡(x,t)|Σ,w⁡(x,t)|Σ,u⁡(⋅,T),v⁡(⋅,T),w⁡(⋅,T)),\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\chi,\xi,F,G,H}(f,g,h)=\big(u(x,t)|_{\Sigma},v(x,t)|_{\Sigma},w(x,t)|_{\Sigma},u(\cdot,T),v(\cdot,T),w(\cdot,T)\big), (1.11)

where the superscript ’++’ emphasizes that we consider non-negative solutions biologically relevant for population densities. The inverse problem is then formulated as:

ℳχ,ξ,F,G,H+→{χ,ξ,F,G,H}.\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\chi,\xi,F,G,H}\to\{\chi,\xi,F,G,H\}. (1.12)

We focus on the fundamental question of unique identifiability: for two parameter configurations A1={χ1,ξ1,F1,G1,H1}A_{1}=\{\chi_{1},\xi_{1},F_{1},G_{1},H_{1}\} and A2={χ2,ξ2,F2,G2,H2}A_{2}=\{\chi_{2},\xi_{2},F_{2},G_{2},H_{2}\}, does

ℳA1+=ℳA2+if and only ifA1=A2​?\mathcal{M}^{+}_{A_{1}}=\mathcal{M}^{+}_{A_{2}}\quad\text{if and only if}\quad A_{1}=A_{2}? (1.13)

A rigorous statement of our main identifiability result is presented in Section 1.3.

For the remainder of this paper, we specialize to the system (1.10) into:

{∂tu=Δu−∇⋅(χu∇v)+∇⋅(ξu∇w)+F(x,u),in​Q,τ​∂tv=Δ​v+G⁡(x,u,v),in​Q,τ​∂tw=Δ​w+H⁡(x,u,w),in​Q,∂νu=∂νv=∂νw=0,on​Σ,u(x,0)=f(x),v(x,0)=g(x),w(x,0)=h(x),in​Ω,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(\chi u\nabla v)+\nabla\cdot(\xi u\nabla w)+F(x,u),&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}v=\Delta v+G(x,u,v),&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}w=\Delta w+H(x,u,w),&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}u=\partial_{\nu}v=\partial_{\nu}w=0,&\ \text{on}\ \Sigma,\\ u(x,0)=f(x),\,v(x,0)=g(x),\,w(x,0)=h(x),&\ \text{in}\ \Omega,\\ \end{cases} (1.14)

where τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\} unifies the parabolic-elliptic and fully parabolic cases. The nonlinear terms assume specific analytic forms:

F⁡(x,m):=r​m−μ​m2,F(x,m):=rm-\mu m^{2}, (1.15)

representing logistic growth with intrinsic rate r>0r>0 and carrying capacity parameter μ>0\mu>0. The functions G⁡(x,m,z),H⁡(x,m,z)G(x,m,z),H(x,m,z) are analytic with respect to mm and z,z, and are of the forms below:

G⁡(x,m,z):=∑p,q=0,p+q>0αp​q​(x)​mp​zq,H⁡(x,m,z):=∑r,s=0,r+s>0βr​s​(x)​mr​zs.G(x,m,z):=\sum\limits_{p,q=0,p+q>0}\alpha^{pq}(x)m^{p}z^{q},\quad H(x,m,z):=\sum\limits_{r,s=0,r+s>0}\beta^{rs}(x)m^{r}z^{s}. (1.16)

This formulation maintains biological relevance while providing sufficient mathematical structure for rigorous analysis of the inverse problem.

We emphasize that the unknown parameters consist of both constants and spatially dependent functions. Specifically, the chemotactic sensitivities χ\chi and ξ\xi, the logistic growth coefficients rr and μ\mu, and the first-order decay rates α01\alpha^{01} and β01\beta^{01} are positive constants. In contrast, the production rates α10​(x)\alpha^{10}(x) and β10​(x)\beta^{10}(x), as well as the higher-order interaction coefficients αp​q​(x)\alpha^{pq}(x) and βr​s​(x)\beta^{rs}(x) for p+q≥2p+q\geq 2 and r+s≥2r+s\geq 2, are functions of the spatial variable xx. The precise structure and admissibility conditions for the coefficients αp​q,βr​s\alpha^{pq},\beta^{rs} are specified in Definitions 1.3 and 1.4.

Furthermore, we clarify that the measurement operator ℳχ,ξ,F,G,H+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{\chi,\xi,F,G,H} corresponds to a full set of boundary and final-time observations generated by varying the initial data (f,g,h)(f,g,h) over an appropriate space of admissible non-negative functions. This framework, often referred to as a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, provides infinitely many measurements, which are necessary for the high-order variation method. The ability to vary the initial data is essential to our approach, as it allows us to isolate individual coefficients by selectively activating or suppressing specific terms in the linearized systems.

We emphasize that our results do not address the single-measurement case, where only one fixed initial datum (f0,g0,h0)(f_{0},g_{0},h_{0}) is prescribed and the corresponding boundary and final-time data are observed. The single-measurement inverse problem is considerably more challenging and requires fundamentally different techniques. In particular, the high-order variation method is no longer applicable, as it relies on the availability of infinitely many measurements corresponding to a family of initial data. To treat the single-measurement case for coupled nonlinear parabolic-elliptic-elliptic systems, one would typically need to employ Carleman estimates to derive stability and uniqueness results from a single observation. We refer to the foundational works of M. Klibanov [17, 3, 16, 18], O. Imanuvilov, M. Yamamoto [35, 9] and their collaborators for the development of Carleman estimate-based methodologies for inverse problems with single measurements. These techniques have been successfully applied to various coefficient inverse problems for parabolic and hyperbolic equations; however, extending them to the mixed parabolic-elliptic-elliptic chemotaxis system considered here remains a substantial open problem due to the nonlinear coupling between equations of different types and the inherent analytical challenges of mixed-type systems. The interplay between time-dependent parabolic dynamics and instantaneous elliptic equilibrium constraints introduces fundamental difficulties that are absent in purely parabolic or purely elliptic settings, making the single-measurement problem for such mixed-type systems particularly challenging.

The primary novelty of our work lies in establishing unique identifiability results for this class of coupled nonlinear chemotaxis systems, addressing a significant gap in the inverse problems literature for biologically relevant PDE models with mixed parabolic-elliptic dynamics.

1.3 Statement of main results

This section is devoted to establishing the mathematical framework and presenting the main results. We begin by introducing several admissible classes for the nonlinearities FF, GG, and HH that appear in systems (1.14). These classes ensure the necessary analytic and structural conditions required for our subsequent analysis. The definitions generalize previous frameworks by allowing expansion around arbitrary non-negative constant solutions and incorporating spatial dependence through multiplicative separability conditions.

Suppose (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) is a known non-negative constant solution of (1.14) and F,G,HF,G,H are analytic. Then, we can introduce the following admissible classes.

Definition 1.1.

Let (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) be a known non-negative constant solution of (1.14). We say that U⁡(x,z):ℝn×ℂ→ℂU(x,z):\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} is admissible, denoted by U∈𝒜,U\in\mathcal{A}, if:

(a) The map z↦U⁡(⋅,z)z\mapsto U(\cdot,z) is holomorphic with value in C02+α​(Ω¯),C^{2+\alpha}_{0}(\bar{\Omega}),

(b) U⁡(x,u0)=0U(x,u_{0})=0 for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega.

It is clear that if UU satisfies these two conditions, it can be expanded into a power series

U⁡(x,z)=∑m=1∞Um​(x)​zmm!,U(x,z)=\sum\limits^{\infty}_{m=1}U_{m}(x)\frac{z^{m}}{m!},

where Um​(x)=∂m∂zm​U​(x,u0)∈C02+α​(Ω)U_{m}(x)=\frac{\partial^{m}}{\partial z^{m}}U(x,u_{0})\in C^{2+\alpha}_{0}(\Omega).

This admissibility condition is imposed by analytically extending UU to a holomorphic function U~\tilde{U} in the complex variable zz and then restricting back to the real line. Since UU is real-valued for real arguments, we assume the coefficients Um​(x)U_{m}(x) are real-valued.

We next define a specific spatial structure required for the subsequent analysis.

Definition 1.2.

We say that a function A⁡(x)A(x) is of multiplicative separable form (with respect to the nn-th spatial variable), if

A⁡(x)=A1​(x1,…,xn−1)​A2​(xn),A(x)=A_{1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1})A_{2}(x_{n}),

for x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) and

∫{xn:(x1,…,xn)∈Ω}A2(xn)dxn≠0.\int_{\{x_{n}:(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\Omega\}}A_{2}(x_{n})dx_{n}\neq 0.
Definition 1.3.

Let (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) be a known non-negative constant solution of (1.14). We say that V⁡(x,p,q):ℝn×ℂ×ℂ→ℂV(x,p,q):\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} is admissible, denoted by V∈ℬ,V\in\mathcal{B}, if:

(a) The map (p,q)↦V⁡(⋅,p,q)(p,q)\mapsto V(\cdot,p,q) is holomorphic with value in C02+α​(Ω¯),C^{2+\alpha}_{0}(\bar{\Omega}),

(b) V⁡(x,u0,v0)=0V(x,u_{0},v_{0})=0 for all x∈Ω,x\in\Omega,

(c) The first-order Taylor coefficient V(0,1)​(x,⋅,v0)V^{(0,1)}(x,\cdot,v_{0}) is constant,

(d) The first-order Taylor coefficient V(1,0)(x,u0,⋅)V^{(1,0)}(x,u_{0},\cdot) is independent of one variable,

(e) The higher-order Taylor coefficient V(k)​(x,⋅,⋅)​(k≥2)V^{(k)}(x,\cdot,\cdot)(k\geq 2) is of a multiplicative separable form for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

It is clear that if VV satisfies these four conditions, it can be expanded into a power series

V⁡(x,p,q)=∑m≥1,n≥0∞Vm​n​(x)​pm​qn(m+n)!,V(x,p,q)=\sum\limits^{\infty}_{m\geq 1,\,n\geq 0}V_{mn}(x)\frac{p^{m}q^{n}}{(m+n)!},

where Vm​n​(x)=∂m∂pm​∂n∂qn​V​(x,u0,v0)∈C02+α​(Ω)V_{mn}(x)=\frac{\partial^{m}}{\partial p^{m}}\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial q^{n}}V(x,u_{0},v_{0})\in C^{2+\alpha}_{0}(\Omega).

Similarly, we can give admissible class for H⁡(x,u,w)H(x,u,w) as:

Definition 1.4.

Let (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) be a known non-negative constant solution of (1.14). We say that W⁡(x,p,q):ℝn×ℂ×ℂ→ℂW(x,p,q):\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} is admissible, denoted by W∈𝒞,W\in\mathcal{C}, if:

(a) The map (p,q)↦W⁡(⋅,p,q)(p,q)\mapsto W(\cdot,p,q) is holomorphic with value in C02+α​(Ω¯),C^{2+\alpha}_{0}(\bar{\Omega}),

(b) W⁡(x,u0,w0)=0W(x,u_{0},w_{0})=0 for all x∈Ω,x\in\Omega,

(c) The first-order Taylor coefficient W(0,1)​(x,⋅,w0)W^{(0,1)}(x,\cdot,w_{0}) is constant,

(d) The first-order Taylor coefficient W(1,0)(x,u0,⋅)W^{(1,0)}(x,u_{0},\cdot) is independent of one variable,

(e) The higher-order Taylor coefficient W(k)​(x,⋅,⋅)​(k≥2)W^{(k)}(x,\cdot,\cdot)(k\geq 2) is of a multiplicative separable form for x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

It is clear that if WW satisfies these four conditions, it can be expanded into a power series

W⁡(x,p,q)=∑m≥1,n≥0∞Wm​n​(x)​pm​qn(m+n)!,W(x,p,q)=\sum\limits^{\infty}_{m\geq 1,\,n\geq 0}W_{mn}(x)\frac{p^{m}q^{n}}{(m+n)!},

where Wm​n​(x)=∂m∂pm​∂n∂qn​W​(x,u0,w0)∈C02+α​(Ω)W_{mn}(x)=\frac{\partial^{m}}{\partial p^{m}}\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial q^{n}}W(x,u_{0},w_{0})\in C^{2+\alpha}_{0}(\Omega).

It can be easily seen that for F∈𝒜,G∈ℬF\in\mathcal{A},G\in\mathcal{B} and H∈𝒞,H\in\mathcal{C}, F,GF,G and HH are of the forms (1.15) and (1.16) respectively.

These definitions generalize the admissibility conditions used in previous biological inverse problems [21, 27]. Unlike [27], which expands around (0,0)(0,0), our framework allows for expansion around any constant solution (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}). Furthermore, compared to [21] which requires constant Taylor coefficients, we allow the coefficients Vm​n​(x)V_{mn}(x) and Wm​n​(x)W_{mn}(x) to be functions of xx, subject to the separability condition, thereby broadening the applicability of our results.

Under these admissibility conditions, we can establish the well-posedness of (1.14). We consider a more general system:

{∂tu=Δu−∇⋅(χu∇v)+∇⋅(ξu∇w)+h(u),in​Q,τ​∂tv=Δ​v+b1​(x,u,v),in​Q,τ​∂tw=Δ​w+b2​(x,u,w),in​Q,∂νu=∂νv=∂νw=0,on​Σ,u(x,0)=f(x),v(x,0)=g(x),w(x,0)=h(x),in​Ω.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(\chi u\nabla v)+\nabla\cdot(\xi u\nabla w)+h(u),&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}v=\Delta v+b_{1}(x,u,v),&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}w=\Delta w+b_{2}(x,u,w),&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}u=\partial_{\nu}v=\partial_{\nu}w=0,&\ \text{on}\ \Sigma,\\ u(x,0)=f(x),\,v(x,0)=g(x),\,w(x,0)=h(x),&\ \text{in}\ \Omega.\\ \end{cases} (1.17)

When τ=1\tau=1, the system (1.17) is fully parabolic. Choosing b1​(x,u,v)=u−vb_{1}(x,u,v)=u-v and b2​(x,u,w)=u−wb_{2}(x,u,w)=u-w, it is known from [11] that if h⁡(u)h(u) satisfies

h∈C1([0,∞)),h(0)≥0,h(s)≤r−μsγ for s≥0,μ,γ>0,r≥0,h\in C^{1}([0,\infty)),\quad h(0)\geq 0,\quad h(s)\leq r-\mu s^{\gamma}\text{ for }s\geq 0,\quad\mu,\gamma>0,\quad r\geq 0,

then (1.17) possesses a global classical solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) under certain conditions (see Theorem 1.1 in [11]).

When τ=0\tau=0, the system (1.17) becomes parabolic-elliptic-elliptic. With b1​(x,u,v)=u−vb_{1}(x,u,v)=u-v, b2​(x,u,w)=u−wb_{2}(x,u,w)=u-w, and h⁡(u)=0h(u)=0, local and global well-posedness results can be established based on Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 in [33]. For the logistic case h⁡(u)=r​u−μ​u2h(u)=ru-\mu u^{2} and with f∈C2+α​(Ω)f\in C^{2+\alpha}(\Omega), a unique local solution exists. Modifying b1b_{1} and b2b_{2} to b1​(x,u,v)=α​u−β​vb_{1}(x,u,v)=\alpha u-\beta v and b2​(x,u,w)=γ​u−δ​wb_{2}(x,u,w)=\gamma u-\delta w, Theorem 1.1 in [36] guarantees a unique, uniformly bounded global classical solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) to (1.17).

These results provide the necessary well-posedness foundation for the applied model (1.5). We now present the main results of this paper concerning the inverse problems. Our goal is to uniquely determine the unknown biological parameters—including the chemotactic sensitivities χ\chi and ξ\xi, the logistic growth coefficients rr and μ\mu, and the coefficients αp​q\alpha^{pq}, βp​q\beta^{pq} (for p,q≥0p,q\geq 0, p+q>0p+q>0) governing the chemical kinetics—from the measurement operator ℳA+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{A}.

Theorem 1.5.

Suppose that the system (1.14) has a solution (u,v,w)∈C01+α2,2+α​(Q)×C01+α2,2+α​(Q)×C01+α2,2+α​(Q)(u,v,w)\in C^{1+\frac{\alpha}{2},2+\alpha}_{0}(Q)\times C^{1+\frac{\alpha}{2},2+\alpha}_{0}(Q)\times C^{1+\frac{\alpha}{2},2+\alpha}_{0}(Q), and coefficients χ\chi and ξ\xi in (1.14), as well as all orders of uu, vv and ww, defined under the notion of high-order variation, are independent of one spatial variable. Assume F∈𝒜,F\in\mathcal{A}, G∈ℬG\in\mathcal{B} and H∈𝒞H\in\mathcal{C} for j=1,2.j=1,2. Let ℳA+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{A} be the associated measurement map as defined in (1.11). For any (f,g,h)∈C2+α​(Ω)×C2+α​(Ω)×C2+α​(Ω)(f,g,h)\in C^{2+\alpha}(\Omega)\times C^{2+\alpha}(\Omega)\times C^{2+\alpha}(\Omega), one has

ℳA1+​(f,g,h)=ℳA2+​(f,g,h),\mathcal{M}^{+}_{A_{1}}(f,g,h)=\mathcal{M}^{+}_{A_{2}}(f,g,h),

then it holds that

A1=A2​in​Ω×ℝ.A_{1}=A_{2}\ \text{in}\ \,\Omega\times\mathbb{R}.

Based on the well-posedness results discussed above, we derive the following corollary for the specific biological system (1.5).

Corollary 1.6.

Let ℳBj+\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B_{j}} (Bj={χj,ξj,rj,μj,αj,βj,γj,δj},j=1,2)(B_{j}=\{\chi_{j},\xi_{j},r_{j},\mu_{j},\alpha_{j},\beta_{j},\gamma_{j},\delta_{j}\},j=1,2) be the measurement map associated to the following system:

{∂tuj=Δuj−∇⋅(χjuj∇vj)+∇⋅(ξjuj∇wj)+rju−μju2,in​Q,τ​∂tvj=Δ​vj+αj​uj−βj​vj,in​Q,τ​∂twj=Δ​wj+γj​uj−δj​wj,in​Q,∂νuj=∂νvj=∂νwj=0,on​Σ,uj(x,0)=f(x),vj(x,0)=g(x),wj(x,0)=h(x),in​Ω.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u_{j}=\Delta u_{j}-\nabla\cdot(\chi_{j}u_{j}\nabla v_{j})+\nabla\cdot(\xi_{j}u_{j}\nabla w_{j})+r_{j}u-\mu_{j}u^{2},&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}v_{j}=\Delta v_{j}+\alpha_{j}u_{j}-\beta_{j}v_{j},&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \tau\partial_{t}w_{j}=\Delta w_{j}+\gamma_{j}u_{j}-\delta_{j}w_{j},&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}u_{j}=\partial_{\nu}v_{j}=\partial_{\nu}w_{j}=0,&\ \text{on}\ \Sigma,\\ u_{j}(x,0)=f(x),\,v_{j}(x,0)=g(x),\,w_{j}(x,0)=h(x),&\ \text{in}\ \Omega.\end{cases} (1.18)

For a given set of parameters βj,δj,χj\beta_{j},\delta_{j},\chi_{j}, and ξj\xi_{j}, suppose there exists a solution (uj,vj,wj)(u_{j},v_{j},w_{j}) to (1.18) that also satisfies the assumptions of Theorem 1.5. If for any f,g,h∈C2+α​(Ω),f,g,h\in C^{2+\alpha}(\Omega), one has

ℳB1+​(f,g,h)=ℳB2+​(f,g,h),\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B_{1}}(f,g,h)=\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B_{2}}(f,g,h),

then it holds that

B1=B2​in​Ω×ℝ.B_{1}=B_{2}\ \text{in}\ \,\Omega\times\mathbb{R}.

1.4 Technical developments and discussion

Our work presents a significant breakthrough by establishing a novel theoretical framework for solving inverse problems in complex biological systems modeled by coupled nonlinear partial differential equations of mixed parabolic-elliptic type.

A primary novelty of our work lies in the first systematic investigation of unique identifiability for a coupled nonlinear system of mixed parabolic-elliptic-elliptic type using only boundary measurements. Previous studies have predominantly focused on systems that are either purely parabolic [4, 10] or purely elliptic [19, 20], leaving a significant gap for hybrid models that arise in complex biological applications.

This mixed-type structure introduces extraordinary theoretical challenges that render conventional techniques inadequate. Unlike purely parabolic or elliptic systems, the coupled model requires fundamentally new approaches to handle the interplay between time-dependent dynamics and instantaneous equilibrium constraints. The inherent analytical complexities are substantial: the nonlinear coupling between equations of different types prevents direct application of standard methods such as energy estimates or perturbation techniques.

A major technical difficulty arises from the fact that while the functions v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) and w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) satisfy elliptic equations, they maintain crucial time dependence through their coupling with the parabolic equation for u⁡(x,t)u(x,t). This temporal dependence directly contradicts the construction of traditional Complex Geometric Optics (CGO) solutions, which typically rely on purely spatial harmonic functions.

To overcome these challenges, we develop a novel methodology that significantly extends existing techniques. Inspired by [28], we introduce a framework capable of handling equations with multiplicative separable spatial structure, particularly coefficients of the form a⁡(x)=a1​(x1,⋯,xn−1)​a2​(xn)a(x)=a_{1}(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n-1})a_{2}(x_{n}) as formalized in Lemma 2.2. A key innovation is the combined use of the fundamental theorem of calculus and the inverse Fourier transform, which enables effective decoupling of temporal and spatial dependencies. This approach provides a unified analytical framework for simultaneous recovery of all unknown model parameters through strategic variation of initial input data, representing a substantial advancement beyond existing methods for inverse problems.

Building upon our previous work on inverse problems in biological systems, this study shifts focus from macroscopic population dynamics to the microscale processes of chemotaxis—where individual cells navigate chemical gradients. While our prior investigations [5, 27, 21, 22, 23] addressed system-level behaviors using purely parabolic models: [21] introduced a high-order variation method to ensure physiologically meaningful solutions and recover source coefficients under admissible classes, and [22] focused on multi-population aggregation systems with recovery of diffusion rates, advection coefficients, and interaction kernels, the current work enters a less charted territory in inverse problems: cell-level mechanism identification. Rather than examining collective outcomes, we target the fundamental signaling and response mechanisms that govern individual cell behavior, an area that remains largely open in the field of parameter identification.

In [24], we began exploring environmental interaction in a 3D chemotaxis-fluid model, though within a purely parabolic framework and with limited parameter recovery. Here, we advance into biologically more realistic settings by incorporating mixed parabolic-elliptic dynamics, which better represent the rapid diffusion of chemical signals relative to cell movement.

This extension is not only mathematically novel but also physiologically critical: it allows us to model how cells process simultaneous attractive and repulsive cues in realistic microenvironments. As in all our studies, we rigorously preserve solution non-negativity to ensure that results remain consistent with biological constraints. By bridging microscopic cell behavior and population-level outcomes, this work offers a more comprehensive mathematical framework for understanding gradient-guided migration in development, immunity, and disease.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present the detailed proof of the main uniqueness theorem (Theorem 1.5). Section 3 is devoted to the proof of the corollary (Corollary 1.6) for the specific biological application model. Additional technical lemmas and supporting results are included in the subsequent sections.

2 PROOF OF THE MAIN THEOREM

This section is devoted to the proof of the main theorem. We begin by establishing two key auxiliary lemmas that play a fundamental role in our analysis.

2.1 Auxiliary lemmas

The first lemma provides a spectral representation of solutions to a linear parabolic system, which will be used to construct specific input data for our inverse problem.

Lemma 2.1.

Consider the system

{∂tu⁡(x,t)−q​Δ​u​(x,t)+k​u​(x,t)=0,in​Q,∂νu⁡(x,t)=0,on​Σ,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u(x,t)-q\Delta u(x,t)+ku(x,t)=0,&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}u(x,t)=0,&\ \text{on}\ \Sigma,\end{cases} (2.1)

First, choose f1​(x)=0f_{1}(x)=0 and g1​(x)>0g_{1}(x)>0. Following a similar reasoning as in the previous proof, it follows that u(I)​(x,t)u^{(I)}(x,t) must be trivial. Consequently, by taking the solution ω⁡(x)\omega(x) of (2.17), from (2.48), we derive:

∫Q2​(α102​(x)−α202​(x))​(v(I)​(x,t))2​ω​(x)​𝑑x​𝑑t=0.\int_{Q}2(\alpha^{02}_{1}(x)-\alpha^{02}_{2}(x))(v^{(I)}(x,t))^{2}\omega(x)dxdt=0. (2.49)

Here we choose the CGO solution for ω⁡(x)\omega(x) to (2.17) as ω⁡(x)=eζ⋅x,\omega(x)=e^{\zeta\cdot x}, where ζ∈ℝ\zeta\in\mathbb{R} is of the form in Lemma 2.2. Then by Lemma 2.2 and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have

(α102​(x)−α202​(x))​(v(I)​(x,tm))2=0,tm∈(0,T).(\alpha^{02}_{1}(x)-\alpha^{02}_{2}(x))(v^{(I)}(x,t_{m}))^{2}=0,\quad t_{m}\in(0,T).

Since g1​(x)>0g_{1}(x)>0, by the maximum principle, v(I)>0v^{(I)}>0. Therefore, it follows that α102​(x)=α202​(x)\alpha^{02}_{1}(x)=\alpha^{02}_{2}(x) in Ω\Omega.

Next, choose g1​(x)=0g_{1}(x)=0 and f1​(x)>0f_{1}(x)>0 to recover α20​(x)\alpha^{20}(x) similarly.

Finally, choose f1​(x),g1​(x)>0f_{1}(x),g_{1}(x)>0, which leads us to u(I),v(I)>0u^{(I)},v^{(I)}>0, and similarly apply Lemma 2.2 to recover α11​(x)\alpha^{11}(x).

Then the equations for v¯(I​I)​(x,t)\bar{v}^{(II)}(x,t) become

{−Δ​v¯(I​I)​(x,t)−α01​v¯(I​I)​(x,t)=0,in​Q,∂νv¯(I​I)​(x,t)=v¯(I​I)​(x,t)=0,on​Σ,v¯(I​I)​(x,0)=v¯(I​I)​(x,T)=0,in​Ω,\begin{cases}-\Delta\bar{v}^{(II)}(x,t)-\alpha^{01}\bar{v}^{(II)}(x,t)=0,&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}\bar{v}^{(II)}(x,t)=\bar{v}^{(II)}(x,t)=0,&\ \text{on}\ \Sigma,\\ \bar{v}^{(II)}(x,0)=\bar{v}^{(II)}(x,T)=0,&\ \text{in}\ \Omega,\end{cases}

which implies v1(I​I)​(x,t)=v2(I​I)​(x,t)v^{(II)}_{1}(x,t)=v^{(II)}_{2}(x,t), denoted as v(I​I)​(x,t)v^{(II)}(x,t).

Recovery of the second-order coefficients of the source term β11​(x),β20​(x)\beta^{11}(x),\beta^{20}(x) and β02​(x)\beta^{02}(x). To recover these three coefficients, we follow a similar approach as we recover α11​(x),α20​(x)\alpha^{11}(x),\alpha^{20}(x) and α02​(x)\alpha^{02}(x).

2.4 Recovery of the higher-order coefficients of the source term

In this subsection, we introduce the high-order variation framework under a more general setting. Inductively, for ℓ∈ℕ,N>2\ell\in\mathbb{N},N>2, we define

uj(ℓ)=∂εℓuj|ε=0,vj(ℓ)=∂εℓvj|ε=0,and​wj(ℓ)=∂εℓwj|ε=0,u^{(\ell)}_{j}=\partial_{\varepsilon}^{\ell}u_{j}|_{\varepsilon=0},\,v^{(\ell)}_{j}=\partial_{\varepsilon}^{\ell}v_{j}|_{\varepsilon=0},\,\text{and}\,w^{(\ell)}_{j}=\partial_{\varepsilon}^{\ell}w_{j}|_{\varepsilon=0},

and obtain a sequence of parabolic-elliptic-elliptic systems for τ=0\tau=0.

The main idea for recovering higher-order coefficients αk1​k2\alpha^{k_{1}k_{2}} and βk1​k2\beta^{k_{1}k_{2}} with k1+k2=k≥3k_{1}+k_{2}=k\geq 3 is mathematical induction, based on the kk-th variation of (2.5).

Thus, the proof is complete. □\hfill{\square}

3 APPLICATIONS

In this section, we apply the above conclusion to an attraction-repulsion chemotaxis system with superlinear logistic degradation. We demonstrate how to recover the coefficients simultaneously under τ=1\tau=1 and τ=0\tau=0.

We recall that the system describes the spatiotemporal dynamics of a biological population uu (e.g., cells, bacteria) interacting with two chemical signals vv (attractant) and ww (repellent). The well-posedness of (1.5) is discussed in subsection 1.3. When τ=1\tau=1, the system is classified as a total parabolic system, while it becomes a parabolic-elliptic-elliptic system when τ=0\tau=0. Given the measurement map in (1.6), we aim to prove Corollary 1.6 from both perspectives: τ=1\tau=1 and τ=0\tau=0.

Proof.

We carry out the proof in two steps, τ=0\tau=0 and τ=1\tau=1.

For the case τ=0\tau=0, it is evident that the system (1.18) is a simpler form of the system (2.5) while αj=αj10\alpha_{j}=\alpha^{10}_{j}, βj=αj01\beta_{j}=\alpha^{01}_{j}, γj=βj10\gamma_{j}=\beta^{10}_{j}, δj=βj01\delta_{j}=\beta^{01}_{j} and all the other αjp​q=βjr​s=0\alpha^{pq}_{j}=\beta^{rs}_{j}=0 for p+q>2p+q>2 and r+s>2r+s>2. Thus, we can conclude that B1=B2B_{1}=B_{2} using the same method as in the main proof.

For the case τ=1\tau=1, the equations (1.18) is a parabolic system, the recovery of the coefficients χj,ξj,rj\chi_{j},\xi_{j},r_{j} and μj\mu_{j} are identical to the above proof. And we recover the coefficient functions αj,βj,γj\alpha_{j},\beta_{j},\gamma_{j} and δj\delta_{j} in a way as in parabolic systems. Without losing generality, we recover αj\alpha_{j} and βj\beta_{j}, the recovery of γj\gamma_{j} and δj\delta_{j} follow an identical approach.

Following the same procedure for constructing high-order variation forms as outlined in Section 2, we derive the first-order variation system for u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) of (1.18) as:

{∂tuj(I)​(x,t)=Δ​uj(I)​(x,t)+rj​uj(I)​(x,t),in​Q,∂tvj(I)​(x,t)=Δ​vj(I)​(x,t)+αj​uj(I)​(x,t)−βj​vj(I)​(x,t),in​Q,∂νuj(I)​(x,t)=∂νvj(I)​(x,t)=0,on​Σ,u(I)j(x,0)=f1(x),v(I)j(x,0)=g1(x),in​Ω.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u^{(I)}_{j}(x,t)=\Delta u^{(I)}_{j}(x,t)+r_{j}u^{(I)}_{j}(x,t),&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \partial_{t}v^{(I)}_{j}(x,t)=\Delta v^{(I)}_{j}(x,t)+\alpha_{j}u^{(I)}_{j}(x,t)-\beta_{j}v^{(I)}_{j}(x,t),\,&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}u^{(I)}_{j}(x,t)=\partial_{\nu}v^{(I)}_{j}(x,t)=0,&\ \text{on}\ \Sigma,\\ u^{(I)}_{j}(x,0)=f_{1}(x),\,v^{(I)}_{j}(x,0)=g_{1}(x),&\ \text{in}\ \Omega.\\ \end{cases} (3.1)

Following the same approach in Section 2, we know that u1(I)​(x,t)=u2(I)​(x,t)u^{(I)}_{1}(x,t)=u^{(I)}_{2}(x,t). We can denote it as u(I)​(x,t)u^{(I)}(x,t), and can express it as eμ​t​l​(x,μ)e^{\mu t}l(x;\mu) based on Lemma 2.1. Let v¯(I)​(x,t)=v1(I)​(x,t)−v2(I)​(x,t)\bar{v}^{(I)}(x,t)=v^{(I)}_{1}(x,t)-v^{(I)}_{2}(x,t), we can obtain the following system based on ℳB1+​(u0,v0,w0)=ℳB2+​(u0,v0,w0)\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B_{1}}(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})=\mathcal{M}^{+}_{B_{2}}(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}):

{∂tv¯(I)​(x,t)−Δ​v¯(I)​(x,t)+β2​v¯(I)​(x,t)=(α1−α2)​u(I)​(x,t)−(β1−β2)​v1(I)​(x,t),in​Q,∂νv¯(I)​(x,t)=v¯(I)​(x,t)=0,on​Σ,v¯(I)​(x,0)=v¯(I)​(x,T)=0,in​Ω.\begin{cases}\partial_{t}\bar{v}^{(I)}(x,t)-\Delta\bar{v}^{(I)}(x,t)+\beta_{2}\bar{v}^{(I)}(x,t)=(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})u^{(I)}(x,t)-(\beta_{1}-\beta_{2})v^{(I)}_{1}(x,t),&\ \text{in}\ Q,\\ \partial_{\nu}\bar{v}^{(I)}(x,t)=\bar{v}^{(I)}(x,t)=0,&\ \text{on}\ \Sigma,\\ \bar{v}^{(I)}(x,0)=\bar{v}^{(I)}(x,T)=0,&\ \text{in}\ \Omega.\end{cases} (3.2)

Let ω\omega be a solution of the following system

−∂tω−Δω+β2ω=0inQ,-\partial_{t}\omega-\Delta\omega+\beta_{2}\omega=0\ \text{in}\ Q, (3.3)

where β2\beta_{2} is an unknown constant, and the CGO solution to ω\omega is easy to seek from (3.3) as

ω=e(|ξ|2+β2)​t−i​ξ⋅x,\omega=e^{(|\xi|^{2}+\beta_{2})t-\mathrm{i}\xi\cdot x}, (3.4)

with i=−1\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{-1} for ξ∈ℝn.\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Then we multiply ω\omega on both sides of (3.2) and carry on integration by parts, we now achieve

∫Q[(α1−α2)​u(I)​(x,t)−(β1−β2)​v1(I)​(x,t)]​ω​𝑑x​𝑑t=0.\int_{Q}\big[(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})u^{(I)}(x,t)-(\beta_{1}-\beta_{2})v^{(I)}_{1}(x,t)\big]\omega dxdt=0. (3.5)

To recover βj\beta_{j}, we can choose f1​(x)=0f_{1}(x)=0, so equations (3.1) indicate u(I)​(x,t)=0u^{(I)}(x,t)=0. And vj(I)​(x,t)v^{(I)}_{j}(x,t) in (3.1) satisfies the form asked in Lemma 2.1 and can be expressed in the form of v(I)​(x,t)=eλ​t​m​(x,λ)v^{(I)}(x,t)=e^{\lambda t}m(x;\lambda), where λ∈ℝn\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and m⁡(x,λ)∈C2​(Ω)m(x;\lambda)\in C^{2}(\Omega). And the equation (3.5) can transform into:

∫0Teλ​te(|ξ|2+β2)​tdt∫Ω(β1−β2)m(x;λ)e−iξ⋅xdx=0,\int^{T}_{0}e^{\lambda t}e^{(|\xi|^{2}+\beta_{2})t}dt\int_{\Omega}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{2})m(x;\lambda)e^{-\mathrm{i}\xi\cdot x}dx=0,

which yields

∫Ω(β1−β2)m(x;λ)e−iξ⋅xdx=0.\int_{\Omega}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{2})m(x;\lambda)e^{-\mathrm{i}\xi\cdot x}dx=0.

Since this holds for any Neumann eigenfunction m⁡(x,λ)m(x;\lambda) of Δ,\Delta, we obtain

β1=β2=:β.\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=:\beta.

Then equation (3.5) only contains the term including u(I)​(x,t)u^{(I)}(x,t). Once again, we substitute the CGO form of ω\omega on both sides of (3.5) and separate the variables:

∫0Teμ​te(|ξ|2+β2)​tdt∫Ω(α1−α2)l(x;λ)e−iξ⋅xdx=0,\int^{T}_{0}e^{\mu t}e^{(|\xi|^{2}+\beta_{2})t}dt\int_{\Omega}(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})l(x;\lambda)e^{-\mathrm{i}\xi\cdot x}dx=0,

which yields

∫Ω(α1−α2)l(x;λ)e−iξ⋅xdx=0.\int_{\Omega}(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})l(x;\lambda)e^{-\mathrm{i}\xi\cdot x}dx=0.

It is known that this holds for any Neumann eigenfunction l⁡(x,μ)l(x;\mu) of Δ,\Delta, we obtain

α1=α2=:α.\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=:\alpha.

Also note that α\alpha can be a function depending on the space variable xx, which does not affect the proving process and simultaneously broadens the field of application. The same reasoning applies to the recovery of γ\gamma and δ\delta.

In this way, we can recover all the coefficient functions in the set BB, and hence finish the proof for Proposition 1.6. ∎
